claims.text: The as-fabricated Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy is a single-phase FCC material with columnar grains and no precipitates.
Elevated-temperature degradation in both oxidizing and reducing atmospheres is governed by sub-critical aluminum supply to the surface.
The baseline aluminum content is insufficient to form a continuous protective Al2O3 scale.
An aluminum content above approximately 0.5 at% enables formation of a continuous, percolating Al2O3 film while retaining a single-phase FCC matrix.
A continuous Al2O3 film impedes oxide-ion and hydrogen ingress.
A continuous Al2O3 film slows outward metal-cation transport.
Increasing aluminum above the proposed threshold will reduce oxidation mass gain by at least 50%.
Increasing aluminum above the proposed threshold will reduce hydrogen-induced mass loss by at least 80%.
The aluminum increase will not induce secondary phases or compromise formability.
The modified alloy differs from the baseline only by an increase in aluminum to 0.8 at% after normalization.
Above approximately 0.5 at% Al, aluminum cations diffuse to the alloy/scale interface rapidly enough for initially separate oxide islands to coalesce.
The resulting Al2O3 film suppresses oxide-growth kinetics by blocking inward oxide-ion transport and outward metal-cation transport.
The Al2O3 film prevents hydrogen attack or suboxide formation in reducing gas.
After 48 hours at 800 °C in air, the Al-enriched alloy will have at least 50% lower mass gain than the baseline.
After 48 hours at 800 °C in flowing hydrogen, the Al-enriched alloy will show no more than 20% mass loss.
The Al-enriched alloy will form a continuous Al2O3 scale less than 5 micrometers thick.
The baseline alloy will form a mixed titanium/chromium oxide scale more than 10 micrometers thick.
The proposed mechanism applies from 700 to 900 °C, oxygen partial pressures of 10^-15 to 0.21 atm, exposure times up to 100 hours, and aluminum contents of 0.2 to 1.0 at%.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis treats the subscripts Al0.2 and Al0.8 as 0.2 and 0.8 at% Al, but normalizing the stated alloy formulas gives approximately 3.64 at% and 13.11 at% Al, respectively. Both are also already above the proposed 0.5 at% threshold.

The hypothesis predicts an at least 80% reduction in hydrogen-induced mass loss relative to baseline, whereas the predicted outcome states an absolute mass loss of no more than 20%, and the falsification rule ambiguously describes this as being compared with alloy A. These are not necessarily equivalent metrics.
The intervention specifies 0.8 at% Al, while the experimental alloy is written as Al0.8Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3, which corresponds to approximately 13.11 at% Al when normalized.
